findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Reconcile AC1 (`--help` is generated and lists flags) with the mandated `add_help=False`: specify how --help is produced (e.g. an explicit --help check that calls parser.format_help(), or use add_help=True while still routing unknown tokens through parse_known_args) so the --help AC is actually reachable.
evidence: AC1: 'CLI write-command parsing goes through argparse and `--help` is generated (verified by running the command's --help and confirming it lists the flags).'
Behavioral fidelity: 'Use `ArgumentParser(add_help=False)` + `parse_known_args()` ... to keep the silent-skip semantics.'
With add_help=False, argparse does not register/handle -h/--help, so `--help` becomes an unrecognized extra that parse_known_args discards silently — no help text is printed.
findings.finding: AC1 requires `--help` to be generated and list the flags, but the behavioral-fidelity section mandates `ArgumentParser(add_help=False)` to preserve silent-skip via parse_known_args. add_help=False disables argparse's built-in --help handler, so --help would fall through as an unrecognized token and be silently skipped rather than printing generated help — the two requirements are in tension and the plan does not reconcile how --help is produced while add_help is disabled.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria (AC1 `--help` is generated) vs Behavioral fidelity ('Use ArgumentParser(add_help=False) + parse_known_args()')
scenarios: Executor runs the CLI with --help to satisfy AC1 but gets no generated help because add_help was disabled for silent-skip.
findings.suggested_fix: State the mechanism: keep add_help=False for parse_known_args silent-skip, and either (a) explicitly detect `-h`/`--help` in the write-command argv and print `parser.format_help()`, or (b) document that --help verification is done via `parser.format_help()` output listing the flags rather than an exit-0 auto-help path.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify how the argparse refactor preserves claim's next-token `--force <reason>` form (claim.py:44-46) DISTINCTLY from transition's `=`-only `--force`, since argparse reproduces neither by default — call out the asymmetry so the two verbs are not accidentally unified.
evidence: claim.py:44-46 `_parse_force`: `nxt = args[i + 1] if i + 1 < len(args) else ""; return nxt if nxt and not nxt.startswith("--") else "(no reason given)"` — claim's bare `--force` DOES consume the next token as the reason

transition.py:175-180: `--force` matches only exact `--force` (bare) or `--force=` prefix; it never consumes the next token — test_transition_force_flag_24f7.py::test_force_does_not_swallow_a_following_token pins this

Plan says '`--force[=<reason>]` reason-carrying bypass … must be preserved exactly' and 'spelled exactly as claim --force' but the two verbs are NOT identical: claim accepts `--force <reason>` (space form), transition does not

argparse: `store` with `nargs='?'` does not consume a following token as the value; `store` requires `=`-or-space but errors on missing — neither matches claim's 'next token unless it starts with --' rule
findings.finding: The behavioral-fidelity section does not address that claim's `--force` consumes the FOLLOWING argv token as its reason, whereas transition's `--force` takes a value only via `=` — an asymmetry argparse does not reproduce with a single spec.
scenarios: An operator runs `rebar claim <id> --force fix-timeout` (space form); post-refactor argparse either errors or drops the reason, silently changing claim's audit note vs today's 'fix-timeout'
Implementer, reading 'preserve exactly' + 'spelled exactly as claim', unifies both verbs onto one argparse `--force` spec and regresses one of them
findings.suggested_fix: Add an explicit note that claim's `_parse_force` and transition's `--force` have DIFFERENT value-attachment rules (claim consumes a following non-`--` token; transition uses `=` only), and prescribe the argparse treatment for each (e.g. a custom action / post-parse handling for claim's space form) rather than a single shared `--force` spec.

tests/unit/test_transition_force_flag_24f7.py lines 127-137: 'assert _force_reason(["--force-c"]) is None' and 'assert _force_reason(["--forc"]) is None', with the docstring: 'No prefix/abbreviation matching ... Ticket 424f pursues the same guarantee for the argparse-based commands via allow_abbrev=False'.
argparse.ArgumentParser resolves EXISTS in the env; its documented default allow_abbrev=True enables prefix matching unless explicitly disabled.

findings.finding: The plan's 'Behavioral fidelity (argparse defaults that MUST be overridden)' section omits argparse's default prefix-abbreviation matching, which the retained direct-caller test asserts must be OFF (allow_abbrev=False). argparse abbreviates long options by default, so '--forc'/'--force-c' would bind to '--force' unless allow_abbrev=False is set on the new parser — contradicting the observed hand-rolled behavior the refactor must preserve.
findings.location: Plan section 'Behavioral fidelity (argparse defaults that MUST be overridden)'; test tests/unit/test_transition_force_flag_24f7.py::test_truncations_are_not_abbreviation_matched
scenarios: An operator (or a stale script) passes '--forc' or '--force-c'; the argparse shim abbreviation-matches it to '--force', silently bypassing a gate — the exact silent-bypass failure mode the retired-flag guard exists to prevent.
test_truncations_are_not_abbreviation_matched fails because the argparse parser abbreviation-matched, contradicting the plan's promise that the direct-caller test passes unchanged.
findings.suggested_fix: In the 'Behavioral fidelity' section, add a fourth bullet: 'Prefix-abbreviation matching is ON by default in argparse and must be disabled — construct every write-command parser with allow_abbrev=False so a truncated long option (e.g. --forc, --force-c) stays an unknown token instead of binding to --force (see test_truncations_are_not_abbreviation_matched).'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State how the refactor preserves `_parse_assignee`'s unconditional next-token capture (claim.py:65-69) — including `--assignee --force` binding '--force' as the value — under argparse's `store`, which behaves differently, or explicitly ratify a change here.
evidence: claim.py:65-69 `_parse_assignee`: `elif a == "--assignee": if i + 1 >= len(args): raise …; assignee = args[i + 1]` — takes the next token verbatim with NO check that it starts with '--', unlike `_parse_force`
Consequence in current code: `--assignee --force` sets assignee='--force' and (because the loop advances i+=2) `--force` is consumed as the value, not parsed as a force flag
argparse `store` would instead treat '--force' as an unrecognised option and (under parse_known_args) leave assignee unset — a different result
findings.finding: The plan does not address claim's `_parse_assignee` unconditionally consuming the next token as the value (no `--`-prefix guard), which argparse's default `store` would not reproduce for `--assignee --force`.
findings.location: Scope > src/rebar/_commands/claim.py; Contract preservation (--assignee None-vs-'' distinction)
scenarios: `rebar claim <id> --assignee --force` today assigns literal '--force' as assignee; post-refactor argparse would not, changing observable behavior and the None-vs-value determination the plan promises to preserve
findings.suggested_fix: Add this edge case to the behavioral-fidelity list and decide/spec whether argparse should replicate the verbatim next-token capture (custom action) or whether this corner is deliberately allowed to change (documented as accepted).

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Resolve the argparse exit-code capability assertion decisively: commit to overriding `ArgumentParser.error()` (subclass) to raise rather than relying on `exit_on_error=False`, which per cpython #103498 / bpo-41255 does not intercept all error paths (e.g. unrecognized-option / missing-value), and drop the ambiguous 'and/or catch SystemExit' hedge.
evidence: Plan text: 'Construct the parser with `exit_on_error=False` and/or catch `SystemExit`/`argparse.ArgumentError` and re-raise as `CommandError(returncode=1)`'

Retrieved: cpython issue #103498 'argparse exits on error even when exit_on_error=False' — 'When ArgumentParser encounters certain errors, it calls self.error(...) which exits, even when exit_on_error is set to False.'
Retrieved: cpython issue #85427 / bpo-41255 'Argparse.parse_args exits on unrecognized option with exit_on_error=False'
Established prior-art pattern (retrieved, cyberangles.org): subclass ArgumentParser and override error() to raise instead of exit — the reliable way to intercept ALL error paths
findings.finding: The plan's capability assertion that argparse's default exit-2 behavior can be overridden to exit 1 'with exit_on_error=False and/or catch SystemExit/argparse.ArgumentError' is only partially correct: exit_on_error=False does not reliably intercept all argparse error paths.
findings.location: Approach > Behavioral fidelity (argparse defaults that MUST be overridden), third bullet ('Value-less-flag and invalid-arg errors exit 1')
scenarios: A value-less flag (e.g. `--force-close` with no value, or a missing required value) hits an argparse error path that self.error()->exits 2 even under exit_on_error=False, yielding exit-2 + auto-usage instead of the required CommandError(returncode=1) with the existing message
The behavioral-fidelity test asserting value-less flag exits 1 fails because the 'and/or catch SystemExit' hedge was implemented as exit_on_error=False alone
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the 'exit_on_error=False and/or catch SystemExit' language with a definite mechanism: subclass ArgumentParser and override error(self, message) to raise CommandError(returncode=1, message=...); note that exit_on_error=False alone is documented as insufficient for unrecognized-option/missing-value paths (cpython #103498, bpo-41255).
